title: Charities help SNAP enrollees find volunteer gigs so they don’t lose benefits | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

When May Rivera started receiving notices from New York City’s Human Resources Administration this spring warning that she was at risk of losing her food stamps, she was confused. The 30-year-old had heard about the work requirements in the “big beautiful bill,” but she had a job as a housekeeper for up to 12 hours a week so she thought she’d be fine.

She didn’t realize that the sweeping law, passed by Republicans last year, broadened the work mandate, and she was not doing enough.

Panic started to set in. Rivera, who has applied to scores of jobs over the past year with no response, thought back to when she temporarily lost her food stamps in 2024 due to a paperwork error. She had to rely on various food pantries to survive and faced having her electricity shut off because she couldn’t afford to both pay bills and buy groceries. She didn’t want to go through that experience again.

Then, Rivera heard on a podcast that volunteering can count towards the work requirement. So she signed up to pack bags and boxes with fruit, vegetables, rice, peanut butter, shelf-stable milk and other goods at the West Side Campaign Against Hunger, which allows her to both maintain her $306 monthly benefit and help others in her community.

“I know what it’s like to face food insecurity,” said Rivera, who loves to bake and is hoping to get a food handler certification so she can broaden her job search. “No matter what, everyone deserves to eat … it’s just a fundamental right as a human being.”

Like Rivera,more low-income Americans enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — known as SNAP, the formal name for food stamps — must now meet the work requirement. And soon, many Medicaid recipients will have to do the same to maintain their health coverage.

Though many enrollees in these safety net programs have jobs, not all are working enough to meet the mandate of 80 hours a month. They can also volunteer, participate in job training programs or go to school to fulfill the requirement. Some can also qualify for exemptions.

Now some cities and states, as well as nonprofit groups, are stepping up efforts to try to connect these folks with volunteer opportunities so they aren’t dropped from the programs.

The work requirement in food stamps is not new. Certain food stamp enrollees have long had to have jobs or participate in other qualifying activities to receive benefits.

The Republicans’ package expanded that existing mandate to parents with older teen children, people ages 55 to 64, veterans, those experiencing homelessness and former foster youth. Plus, the law made it harder for states to receive waivers during tough economic times.

Some2.4 million fewer Americansare expected to receive food stamps benefits in an average month because of the work mandate provision, according to a Congressional Budget Office analysis released in August 2025.

On top of that, the first-ever federal work mandate in Medicaid will begin in January, though states can opt to delay enforcing it until July. More than 5 million more people are expected to be uninsured in 2034 due to the provision, CBO estimates.

Many enrollees in these safety net programs don’t realize that volunteering allows them to satisfy the mandate. It’s an important alternative, considering many peoplehave part-time jobs with variable hours and others can’t land employment at all.

States differ widely in how well they inform food stamp recipients of the volunteer option, according to a July analysis by the Food Research & Action Center, a left-leaning advocacy group. It found that 20 states do not mention volunteering on their SNAP website, while 27 states and the District of Columbia do. Another three states just make it partially clear.

Adding to the confusion, some states use an alternate calculation — a household’s monthly benefit divided by the local minimum wage — to determine how many hours an enrollee must volunteer each month.

New York is one of those states, which meansRiveraneeds to volunteer18 hours a month on top of her housekeeping job.

Some government agencies and community groups are trying to raise awareness of the volunteer option and to aid enrollees in finding spots. Many of the efforts are still in the early stages and have assisted relatively few people, but the organizers hope to expand their reach over time.

Pennsylvania’s Department of Human Services decided to harness its PA Navigate site — which provides residents with information about charitable food, clothing, job training and other services in their area — to point food stamp recipients to volunteer options. They just type in their zip code and search for “volunteer opportunity.”

“A lot of the Pennsylvanians that we serve through both SNAP and Medicaid have hourly jobs, and they do not always have the ability to increase those hours,” the state agency’s secretary, Valerie Arkoosh, told CNN. “Our goal was to help make sure people understand that by doing some volunteer work, they could complete that 80-hour minimum commitment and be able to securely maintain their benefits.”

Since the volunteer search function launched last November, it’s been used more than 4,500 times.

There were 77 opportunities listed at the end of September, and the number is growing, Arkoosh said. They include working on art projects with people with intellectual disabilities in Philadelphia or stocking inventory at a civic association in Lancaster.

The state is working with the Community Action Association of Pennsylvania, which supports a state-wide network of local organizations, to add more nonprofits and their volunteer opportunities to PA Navigate. The association has a team of community engagement managers, who are educating the groups on the volunteer component of the work requirement and the ability to list any spots they have on the site, said Beck Moore, the association’s CEO.

Still, some people have failed to satisfy the expanded mandate. Some 123,000 Pennsylvania enrollees have lost their food stamps as of the end of September, Arkoosh said.

Some volunteer opportunities can lead to paid jobs at the nonprofits or at other employers.

The Houston Food Bank partners with local job training programs that refer SNAP enrollees to volunteer spots. So far this year, 12 people have fulfilled the work requirement at the food bank, said Lakesha Oludare, the nonprofit’s community service program manager.

Oludare also tries to place them in positions within the food bank where they can gain employment skills. Seven of them landed jobs — including two in a warehouse and two in offices — after volunteering in similar roles at the food bank.

Oludare is looking to increase the number of SNAP participants referred to the food bank by job training programs to as many as 50 people by March.

“Besides assisting them in meeting the work requirements through volunteering, I want them to obtain some kind of primary employment to put them in a position so they don’t have to rely on SNAP benefits,” she said.

In New York City, the Human Resources Administration has created several resources for SNAP participants who want to turn to volunteering to meet the work requirement.

The stakes are high — some 26,500 have already been dropped from the safety net program since March, when the expanded work requirements took effect in the state. Plus, 900,000 Medicaid recipients are at risk of losing their coverage once the work requirement starts next year.

The city agencyset up two ways for nonprofit groups to assist food stamp recipients in logging their volunteer hours. One allows organizations to enter into an agreement with the city to host volunteers and report their hours. The other enables the nonprofit to register as a verified site where enrollees can volunteer and have their hours confirmed, though the recipient is responsible for submitting the paperwork to the agency.

HRA created amapwhere food stamp enrollees can find dozens of volunteer opportunities across the five boroughs. And it has partnered with NYC Service, a division of the Mayor’s Office, which lists volunteer spots at 1,200 organizations around the city. In September, NYC Serviceadded a tabon its sitegeared for food stamp recipients seeking to meet their work requirements, which currently has more than 200 listings.

“For us it was a no brainer to just look at: How do we make our site even more accessible, make things clear for people who are seeking hours for SNAP and Medicaid, making the process as easy as possible,” said Laura Rog, NYC Service’s chief service officer.

HRA said it does not yet have information on how many food stamp enrollees have been connected to volunteer opportunities, while NYC Service doesn’t track why people are signing up for listings.

City Harvest, the largest food rescue organization in the Big Apple, now has 35 SNAP enrollees who volunteer to meet the work mandate. The number of shifts they’ve worked has grown from nine in August to 123 in October, said Alex Guyton, senior manager of volunteer programs.

“There are a lot more folks now facing this requirement and needing to go through this process to tick that box and maintain access to these really crucial benefits,” Guyton said.

The enrollees pack bags of fresh produce and build pallets in the group’s Brooklyn food rescue center for distribution to more than 400 pantries, soup kitchens and other food programs. They have also supported City Harvest’s food distribution efforts on Staten Island, where the nonprofit has had a difficult time finding enough volunteers.

Tonia Lykes, who started receiving food stamps earlier this year after her unemployment benefits ran out, spends a total of 10 hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays building pallets with shelf-stable food like peanut butter, rice, pasta and cooking oil at City Harvest’s rescue center. She also volunteers twice a week at a food pantry in Brooklyn.

Lykes, 56, was not aware of the work requirement until she started receiving letters from HRA earlier this year saying she was not compliant. She reached out to her job training programcounselor, who suggested volunteering. She’s thankful for that option since she’s had little luck in finding a job, despite having worked in the restaurant industry for more than 20 years. Food stamps are a lifeline.

“I don’t have to worry about where my next meal is coming from,” the New York City resident said.

While the focus to date has largely been on food stamp recipients, it will soon broaden to include Medicaid enrollees. Some nonprofits are already preparing.

Greg Silverman, CEO of the West Side Campaign Against Hunger, said he is very concerned about people losing their health coverage. So the group — which already has had 50 food stamp recipients volunteer more than 1,500 hours since March — is planning to make more slots available for those who need to fulfill the work mandate.

“We’re ramping up, and we’ll continue to do more and more outreach and provide more and more opportunities for New Yorkers in need to maintain their benefits,” he said.
